source.title: Provable Target Sample Complexity Improvements as Pre-Trained Models Scale
source.authors: Kazuto Fukuchi; Ryuichiro Hataya; Kota Matsui

record.tranche_reason: The study tests downstream performance across pre-trained model sizes and adapter depths using a different setup from the original language-model held-out-loss scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law results from other work, which are not rows here. Its own experiments report downstream error rates for CNN adaptation and vision-language models, but do not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly theoretical. Its small experiments compare downstream target-domain error at two pre-trained model sizes: ResNet-50 (26M) vs Wide ResNet-50-2 (68M) on Office-Home clipart, and SigLIP Base (86M) vs Large (303M) encoders in a VLM on MMStar. That bears weakly on V6 in a new setting (adapter-based adaptation). It is only two sizes per setting, with no curve and no relation to pretraining loss. No experiment measures pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors prove that caulkability by adapter classes of decreasing complexity is a sufficient condition for downstream sample complexity to improve as pre-training scale grows, as a theoretical justification of empirical transfer scaling laws. They say their experiments corroborate that larger pre-trained models can be adapted with simpler adapters. The CNN result is stated tentatively ('can suggest').
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes adapter-based downstream adaptation and evaluates error rates across model sizes and adapter depths; it does not use the original held-out language-model loss scaling procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported CNN interpretation depends on adapter depth: the larger CNN is described as performing better with a single-layer adapter, while the smaller CNN requires a more complex adapter.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory: if the pre-trained model allows caulking with adapter classes whose complexity shrinks with source sample size m, the target-sample error rate improves toward n^(-2αβ/(2αβ+1)) as m grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger or better pre-trained models improve the downstream sample-complexity exponent (a theoretical account of transfer scaling).

fits_no_version.finding: Experiments suggest the smaller CNN needs a deeper adapter to reach its best error, while the larger one does best with one layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The adapter complexity needed for downstream adaptation decreases with pre-trained model size.

record.problems: The experiment results are shown in figures without layer-specific numerical values in the text. CNN results report the best validation results over five random seeds, and the vision-language experiment reports best test accuracy, but no uncertainty estimates are given. The CNN comparison involves architectures with different parameter counts, so scale is not isolated from architecture.

untested.parts: Predictability (any fitted curve or trend over more than two sizes); dependence on pretraining loss; the VLM size comparison as stated in text; whether the larger model's advantage holds at each adapter depth.
All; no pretraining loss is measured.
All; no power-law fit is made in image or fine-tuning settings.

missing.what: Per-model, per-depth error values and the marked minimum errors (⋆) for the CNNs, and the corresponding VLM values, which are needed to compare downstream error across sizes

record.verdict_notes: Mostly a theory paper; it cites Kaplan, Henighan and Mikami for the scaling laws themselves. The experimental evidence on V6 is minimal: two sizes per setting, with best validation result over 5 seeds (CNN) and best test accuracy (VLM), and no uncertainty reported. The appendix also lists the same SigLIP checkpoint name twice (siglip2-base-patch16-224), so the 'Large' encoder identity is unclear. The reader's limits_scope label was dropped because it rested only on rows whose values cannot be read from the text.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss and its dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at a fixed parameter count and their effect on loss.
Whether the same power-law form holds across other modalities or training regimes.
The experiments measure downstream error by model/encoder size and adapter depth; they do not test predictability from pretraining loss or establish a general scaling curve.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bending of scaling curves.

relationships.condition: CNNs on Office-Home clipart with a single-layer adapter: ResNet-50 (26M) vs Wide ResNet-50-2 (68M)
relationships.reason: Authors say the larger model achieves higher performance with a single-layer adapter (r4 vs r1). This is weak support: two models, size confounded with width, and hedged wording.
relationships.display_finding: Wide ResNet-50-2 achieved higher performance than ResNet-50, although the comparison changed both parameter count and width.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
